title: ‘It’s not about the Qur’an, it’s about the money’: how boys of five are made to beg on Senegal’s streets

paragraphs.en: In a bare, gloomy room on the beachfront at Saint-Louis, in the north-west of Senegal, dozens of young boys sit on a concrete floor chanting verses from the Qur’an, surrounded by fishing boats and piles of rubbish. It is early in the morning but the children have already been up for hours, not to study but to walk the streets begging for food and money.
paragraphs.zh: 在塞内加尔西北部圣路易海滨一间简陋昏暗的房间里，几十名男孩坐在水泥地上背诵《古兰经》经文，周围是渔船和成堆的垃圾。虽然还是清晨，孩子们却已经起床好几个小时了，不是为了学习，而是上街乞讨食物和钱财。

paragraphs.en: Every day, these talibés , or students of the Qur’an, join thousands of other boys, some as young as five, on the streets of the city in search of a piece of baguette, a handful of rice or a few coins. They beg not just to fill their own stomachs but also the pockets of their Qur’anic teachers, or marabouts .
paragraphs.zh: 每天，这些“塔利贝”（talibés，即《古兰经》学生）与成千上万的其他男孩一起，出现在这座城市的大街小巷，乞求一块法棍面包、一把米饭或几个硬币。最小的孩子只有五岁。他们乞讨不仅是为了填饱自己的肚子，也是为了填满他们的《古兰经》老师（或称“马拉布特”）的口袋。

paragraphs.en: Talibés are sent by their parents from impoverished rural regions of Senegal, and as far away as the Gambia and Guinea-Bissau, in the belief they will get an education in Qur’anic schools, known as daaras , in the country’s cities. Many marabouts care for their students but, far from the watchful eyes of their families, others are sent out on to the streets in a practice that human rights groups say amounts to human trafficking for forced begging.
paragraphs.zh: 塔利贝由父母从塞内加尔贫困的农村地区送来，有的甚至来自遥远的冈比亚和几内亚比绍，父母相信他们会在城市里的《古兰经》学校（称为“达拉斯”）接受教育。许多马拉布特善待学生，但也有一些在远离家人视线的地方把孩子打发到街上乞讨——人权组织称，这种做法相当于为了强迫乞讨而进行的人口贩运。

paragraphs.en: Talibés prepare to study the Qur’an under a marabout , or religious teacher, at a daara, or Qur’anic school, in Saint-Louis
paragraphs.zh: 在圣路易的一所达拉（《古兰经》学校），塔利贝们在马拉布特（宗教教师）的指导下准备研习《古兰经》

paragraphs.en: “It’s a business,” says Issa Kouyaté, founder of Maison de la Gare , a Senegalese organisation that provides support, healthcare and education to talibés in Saint-Louis. “It’s not about the Qur’an – it’s about the money.”
paragraphs.zh: “这是一门生意，”伊萨·库亚特（Issa Kouyaté）说。他是塞内加尔组织“车站之家”（Maison de la Gare）的创始人，该组织为圣路易的塔利贝提供支持、医疗和教育。“这与《古兰经》无关——只与钱有关。”

paragraphs.en: Sending children to study under Qur’anic teachers is an old and deeply embedded tradition in Senegal and much of west Africa. Yet, with the onset of urbanisation, the practice shifted from schools, supported by the local community, to daaras in far-off cities – where some marabouts spotted an opportunity to make money from children rather than educate them.
paragraphs.zh: 送孩子到《古兰经》教师门下学习是塞内加尔乃至西非大部分地区一项古老且根深蒂固的传统。然而，随着城市化进程的推进，这种做法从由当地社区支持、设在本地学校的模式，转变为送往遥远城市的达拉——在那里，一些马拉布特发现可以从孩子身上赚钱，而不是教育他们。

paragraphs.en: Talibés recite the Qur’an at a daara in Saint-Louis. The oral tradition, of listening to a teacher and repeating verses aloud, is the accepted method of learning scripture across the Muslim world
paragraphs.zh: 塔利贝们在圣路易的一所达拉背诵《古兰经》。聆听教师讲解、大声重复经文的传统，是整个穆斯林世界学习经文公认的方法

paragraphs.en: Talibés on the streets of Saint-Louis. Despite the treatment they endure, these boys are resilient, energetic and street smart. Children are taught French as part of a residential programme run by Maison de la Gare, a secular Senegalese charity that provides support, healthcare and education to talibés in Saint-Louis
paragraphs.zh: 圣路易街头的塔利贝们。尽管遭受这样的待遇，这些男孩依然坚韧、精力充沛且通晓街头世故。作为“车站之家”住宿项目的一部分，孩子们会学习法语。“车站之家”是一家世俗的塞内加尔慈善机构，为圣路易的塔利贝提供支持、医疗和教育
